title: The breastplate
hookLine: I bind unto myself today the strong name of the Trinity
tomorrow: so many saints and poets. which voice stays with you?

cards: Jacket, keys, phone, earbuds: the gear that goes on before the door. An old Irish prayer is put on like that. “I bind unto myself today the strong Name of the Trinity.”
Some people sing it as a hymn; some pray it while getting dressed. Tradition ties it to Patrick and calls it his breastplate, a prayer worn like armor. So what is armor like that guarding?

teach.b: Its old name is the Lorica, Latin for breastplate, and the picture is older than Ireland. Paul tells the Thessalonians to put on “the breastplate of faith and love.”
The prayer surrounds the wearer: Christ with me, before me, behind me, in me, beneath me, above me. Then it turns outward. Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me.
Christ in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me.
Christ in every eye that sees me.
That's the surprise: the armor doesn't only keep harm out. It changes how the wearer sees everyone else, even the face they're dreading.
Now hold the week up. A young nun carried up in a lift. Love at the heart of the body.
A peaceful spirit that reaches thousands. Thanks before everything. A morning fire with the foe on its guest list.
And today, Christ in every face.

how: Some Christians pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate in the morning, and the hymn version, I bind unto myself today, is sung in some churches.

o: the armor an Irish king wore into battle against raiders
the vestment a priest wears over the chest during Mass
an old prayer worn like armor, asking for Christ in every face

p: the breastplate of faith and love

s: the breastplate prayer is only about keeping harm away
it turns outward too: Christ in every eye that sees me.
Paul writes of a breastplate of faith and love
to the Thessalonians. the Irish prayer takes up the same picture.
the breastplate prayer appears in Patrick's Confession
tradition ties the prayer to Patrick, but it isn't in his Confession.

games.q: your mom prays Saint Patrick's Breastplate before a meeting with a coworker she can't stand. which part might surprise her?
o: asking God to keep that coworker out of her way all day.
asking for Christ in the eyes of the very people she'll face.
a promise that the meeting will go the way she wants.
games.why: the prayer surrounds the wearer, then turns outward: Christ in every eye that sees me, the hard faces included.

practice: Bring three faces to mind that you'll see soon: one easy, one hard, one a stranger. Over each, say the line quietly out loud, Christ in every eye that sees me, or simply say the person's name with a wish for their good.
Let the hard face stay a little longer than the others.

wordCard.voice: The breastplate. The prayer tradition gives to Patrick, worn like armor, asking for Christ on every side and in every face.

orig.note: Latin for breastplate, the prayer's old name.

carryVoice: One more line for the week: Christ in every eye. Armor that changes how you see. Another week, done.
